title: ITERTL An Iterative Framework for Fine-tuning LLMs for RTL Code Generation

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Equation 6 is written as min_π Σ_j -log P_π(a_j|s,a_<j) = min_π Σ_j log (P_teacher(a_j|s,a_<j) / log P_π(a_j|s,a_<j)). The denominator must be P_π, not log P_π; as written the expression is mathematically wrong (and would not even be a log-ratio). Additionally, the first line is not an equality but only an argmin-equivalence (the two expressions differ by the constant Σ_j log P_teacher), despite the text asserting 'The first equality holds because P_teacher is independent of π'.

predicted_errors.error_location: Equation (6), second line: '= min_π Σ_j KL(P_teacher,j || P_π,j)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A per-sample sum of token-level log-ratios for one sampled sequence a is not equal to the sum of KL divergences; KL requires an expectation over the token distribution. The derivation writes this as a strict equality and then, in the next line, applies the law of large numbers again ('the approximate equality in the third line is based on the law of large numbers') to an expression that has already been (incorrectly) turned into an expectation, double-counting the averaging step.

The paper states 'to mitigate random errors, the model is prompted to generate responses with temperature = {0 (greedy decoding), 0.2, 0.5, 0.8} ... For each test metric (pass@1, pass@5, and pass@10), the best result is chosen.' Selecting the maximum over four decoding configurations on the evaluation benchmark does not 'mitigate random errors' — it systematically inflates the reported scores (a best-of-N selection on the test set), and it contradicts the preceding sentence that pass@1 is measured 'under greedy decoding'. Baseline numbers are quoted from [10] and [12] without such per-metric best-of-four tuning, making the comparison unfair.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2 (bottleneck discussion) vs. Section 3.1 (quality score definition)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 3.1 states the quality score z is computed 'utilizing Pyverilog and Rough-L [Rouge-L] following [12]', i.e. it combines syntax checking with reference similarity. Section 3.2 then asserts 'the surrogate reward function r_π evaluates code quality merely from a syntax perspective', contradicting the method description and misstating the reward actually used.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.1 'Training Details' ('total number of iterations is set to 7') vs. Section 4.2 / Figure 2 discussion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Training details say the final model is trained for 7 iterations, yet the analysis states 'From the fifth to the seventh iteration, the pass@1 rate gradually decreases.' Thus the headline results (42.9% / 62.2% pass@1) cannot correspond to the described 7-iteration final model; they apparently come from the best (5th) iteration. The reported configuration and the reported numbers are inconsistent, and selecting the best iteration on the benchmark is itself test-set selection.

'the loss value can still decrease by leveraging newly sampled data points from updated model, validating the effectiveness of the proposed iterative training approach.' A decreasing training loss computed on samples drawn from the model itself is expected by construction (the model assigns higher likelihood to its own outputs) and is not evidence of improved code-generation capability — particularly since the paper also reports that pass@1 declines after the 5th iteration while the loss keeps decreasing.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2 ('surpasses RTLCoder ... by 1% and 1.3%', 'comprehensively surpasses', 'significantly outperforms')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A 1.0 and 1.3 percentage-point margin on benchmarks of 143 and 156 problems corresponds to roughly 1–2 additional solved problems, obtained after taking the best over four decoding temperatures and (implicitly) the best training iteration. Describing this as outperforming the SOTA open-source model 'significantly' / state-of-the-art attainment is not supported by the reported evidence, and no variance or significance analysis is provided.

The caption states 'The results of RTLCoder come from [12]', but the compared variant 'RTLCoder-DeepSeek-10k' (RTLCoder trained with only 10k reference samples) is not a configuration reported in [12]; it must be a baseline retrained by the authors. Attributing it to [12] misrepresents the source of the baseline numbers and hides the training protocol used for this key comparison.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, 'Each response a^t_K is assigned a quality score z^t_k'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The subscript is inconsistent with the rest of the method: a^t_K denotes only the single reference response from π_teacher, yet it is said to receive the K quality scores z^t_k used in the ranking loss (Eq. 2), which requires a score per candidate a^t_k. As written, the scoring step does not match the loss definition.
